Juvenile Catostomus santaanae emerge from the gravel substrate as prolarvae measuring approximately 0.7 centimeters  in total length at hatch, a diminutive size that reflects the limited yolk reserves provisioned within the demersal egg. Following the resorption of the yolk sac and the transition to exogenous feeding, these young-of-year begin a period of rapid somatic growth that continues through their first summer. Under the prevailing thermal regime of southern California streams, reported at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the interval from birth to the attainment of sexual maturity spans approximately 292 days [tp = approximately 292 days], a duration that aligns with field observations indicating that puberty is reached in the second summer of life. By this developmental milestone, individuals have typically achieved a total length at puberty of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 2 grams [Wwp = 2 grams]; indeed, no female measuring under 49 mm in length or weighing less than 2.05 g was found to contain eggs in surveys of the population.

Fecundity estimates for Catostomus santaanae were derived from histological examination of ovarian tissue sampled from six females spanning a size range of 77.8 to 158.2 mm in total length. Under a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the analysis indicated an annual reproductive output of approximately 16,151 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 16,151 eggs per year], a rate consistent with the reproduction rate recorded at a total length of 15 centimeters. This relatively modest per capita fecundity, equating to roughly 44 eggs per day when averaged over the year, aligns with the life-history strategy of a small-bodied catostomid inhabiting hydrologically variable stream environments, where iteroparity and the spread of reproductive effort across multiple spawning events may buffer against recruitment failures in unfavorable years. As females grow, their absolute fecundity increases, but the population-level fecundity schedule remains tightly linked to the size structure of the breeding stock, with larger gravid individuals contributing disproportionately to the annual egg complement.

The ultimate total length recorded for Catostomus santaanae reaches approximately 25 centimeters [Li = approximately 25 centimeters], a maximum size that corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 177.7 grams [Wwi = 177.7 grams] based on the length-weight scaling relationship derived for this species. This asymptotic size is modest compared to many other members of the family Catostomidae, reflecting the constraints imposed by the relatively small, fragmented coastal stream habitats the Santa Ana sucker occupies. The largest individuals are typically females, consistent with the pattern of sexually dimorphic growth common among iteroparous teleosts. Under the temperature conditions prevalent in its native range (13 °C [T = 13 °C]), the lifespan of this species is estimated at approximately 1460 days [am = approximately 1460 days], a longevity that allows for multiple reproductive bouts over the course of an individual's life and underscores the iteroparous nature of its reproductive strategy.

Newly emerged larvae of Catostomus santaanae are notably small, with a wet weight at birth of 0.0056 grams [Wwb = 0.0056 grams], a value derived from the volume of the fertilized ovum assuming an egg diameter of 2.2 mm. This minimal neonatal mass places the species at the lower end of the range observed within the genus, necessitating a rapid onset of exogenous feeding once the yolk reserves are exhausted. At 1.48 centimeters [Lb = 1.48 centimeters] total length at birth, the transition from the encapsulated embryonic stage to the free-swimming larval phase begins, requiring immediate access to suitable prey items in the stream drift. The combination of a small body size at hatching and a relatively short yolk-sac stage imposes a narrow window for successful first feeding, linking early survival closely to the seasonal timing of zooplankton blooms in the stream drift.

Among the native freshwater fishes of coastal southern California, the Santa Ana sucker occupies a distinctive trophic niche as a benthic grazer, feeding predominantly on periphyton and detritus in shallow runs and riffles. This feeding specialization, coupled with its relatively small adult body size of up to 25 centimeters [Li = up to 25 centimeters] total length and a maximum lifespan of approximately 1,460 days [am = approximately 1,460 days], shapes a life history that is closely attuned to the Mediterranean-type seasonal hydrology of its stream ha at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]bitats. Winter and early spring high flows provide spawning cues and transport dispersing larvae downstream, while the receding flows of summer concentrate food resources in isolated pools. The species' iteroparous spawning strategy, with annual fecundity reaching roughly 16,151 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 16,151 eggs per year] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], represents an adaptation to variable recruitment success: by spreading reproductive effort across multiple years, the population buffers itself against the occasional complete failure of a year class during extreme drought or flood events.
